title: Require clinical safety review and crisis-escalation protocols before deploying a chatbot to an emotionally vulnerable user population
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on two chatbot failures affecting emotionally vulnerable users: NEDA's Tessa chatbot giving harmful advice to eating-disorder patients, and the Character.AI wrongful-death lawsuit alleging inadequate safeguards for a minor user. Not a documented decision of any specific organisation.

history.note: Initial Edition 1.1 content, part of the Phase 3 canonical expansion.

decision_statement: Before deploying a chatbot in a mental-health-adjacent context, or to a user base known to include emotionally vulnerable individuals or minors, the organisation must complete a clinical safety review of the chatbot's responses to crisis-adjacent input, implement a crisis-escalation protocol that connects the user to a trained human, and never replace a trained human crisis responder with an unsupervised chatbot.
decision_context: Motivated by NEDA's Tessa chatbot giving calorie-restriction advice to users describing eating-disorder symptoms after replacing a human helpline, and the Character.AI wrongful-death lawsuit alleging a companion chatbot fostered unhealthy dependency in a minor without adequate crisis-intervention mechanisms.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Vulnerable-User AI Safety Board
alternatives_considered: Deploy a chatbot broadly and rely on user reports to surface harmful responses after the fact.
Treat a chatbot as a low-risk supplement to human support without requiring a dedicated clinical safety review.

citations.title: Chatbot that offered bad advice for eating disorders taken down
Garcia v. Character Technologies, Inc. et al., 6:2024cv01903
citations.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this incident.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.

Failing to provide adequate safety safeguards for a product used by a known vulnerable population is squarely the kind of unfair practice this control's authority addresses — the FTC's own 6(b) inquiry into AI companion chatbots confirms this application, so a new control would inflate the mapping without adding meaning.
Compliance must be demonstrated by a documented crisis-escalation protocol test.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether a trained human is actually reachable in a crisis.
